title: In which cases does @Transactional NOT roll back (checked exceptions, self-invocation, private methods, swallowed exceptions), and what are the common pitfalls?

s1_definition.profdef: `@Transactional` does NOT rollback in four cases: (1) **Checked exceptions** — only `RuntimeException`/`Error` trigger rollback by default; a `throws IOException` COMMITS. Fix: `rollbackFor=Exception.class`. (2) **Self-invocation** — calling a `@Transactional` method from within the SAME class bypasses the proxy because `this.method()` goes directly to the real object. Fix: extract to a separate `@Service` bean. (3) **Private methods** — CGLIB cannot override `private`. The annotation is silently ignored. Fix: make `public`. (4) **Swallowed exceptions** — `catch(Exception e) { log.error(...); }` without re-throwing means the proxy sees a successful return → COMMITS. Fix: re-throw or call `TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly()`.
s1_definition.analogy: (1) The vault door only auto-closes on FIRE alarms (RuntimeException), not on SMOKE alarms (checked exceptions). (2) If a teller asks HIMSELF to lock the vault, he just talks to himself — the vault door mechanism (proxy) never activates. (3) The vault door only works on PUBLIC doors, not private ones. (4) If a teller catches the fire alarm and silences it, the vault door thinks everything is fine and stays open (commits).
s1_definition.oneliner: Checked = commits. Self-invocation = no proxy. Private = ignored. Swallowed exception = commits. Fix: rollbackFor, extract bean, make public, re-throw.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Transactional` does NOT rollback in four cases: (1) **Checked exceptions** — only `RuntimeException`/`Error` trigger rollback by default; a `throws IOException` COMMITS. Fix: `rollbackFor=Exception.class`. (2) **Self-invocation** — calling a `@Transactional` method from within the SAME class bypasses the proxy because `this.method()` goes directly to the real object. Fix: extract to a separate `@Service` bean. (3) **Private methods** — CGLIB cannot override `private`. The annotation is silently ignored. Fix: make `public`. (4) **Swallowed exceptions** — `catch(Exception e) { log.error(...); }` without re-throwing means the proxy sees a successful return → COMMITS. Fix: re-throw or call `TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly()`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** (1) The vault door only auto-closes on FIRE alarms (RuntimeException), not on SMOKE alarms (checked exceptions). (2) If a teller asks HIMSELF to lock the vault, he just talks to himself — the vault door mechanism (proxy) never activates. (3) The vault door only works on PUBLIC doors, not private ones. (4) If a teller catches the fire alarm and silences it, the vault door thinks everything is fine and stays open (commits).

**One line to remember:** Checked = commits. Self-invocation = no proxy. Private = ignored. Swallowed exception = commits. Fix: rollbackFor, extract bean, make public, re-throw.

sections.s2_technical:
There are four silent ways a `@Transactional` method fails to roll back. First, checked exceptions: by default the proxy rolls back only on `RuntimeException` and `Error`, so a method declaring `throws PaymentGatewayException` COMMITS even on failure, leaving half-finished data. The fix is `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` so checked exceptions also trigger rollback. Second, self-invocation: calling a transactional method from inside the same class with `this.method()` goes straight to the real object and skips the proxy, so no transaction starts. The fix is to move that method into a separate `@Service` bean and call it through the injected reference.

Third, private methods: Spring Boot uses CGLIB, which proxies by subclassing, and a subclass cannot override a `private` method, so the annotation is silently ignored. The fix is to make the method at least `public`. Fourth, swallowed exceptions: if you write `catch (Exception e) { log.error(...); }` without re-throwing, the proxy sees a normal return and COMMITS the partial work. The fix is to re-throw, or to call `TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly()` so the transaction is marked for rollback even though you handled the exception. A senior nuance: the checked-exception and self-invocation traps cause silent data corruption, so adding `rollbackFor = Exception.class` and extracting beans are standard defensive habits.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's EMI payment service has all 4 rollback pitfalls in one class.** (1) `processEmi()` throws a checked `PaymentGatewayException` — TX commits with partial data. (2) `processAll()` calls `this.processEmi()` — proxy bypassed, no TX. (3) `@Transactional` on a private helper — silently ignored. (4) Exception caught and logged but not re-thrown — TX commits with corrupted state. Each pitfall demonstrated with fix.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: EMI-001 for Rajesh's loan, processed through the fixed service where the payment gateway returns a checked failure.

**Step 1.** The controller calls the fixed service method annotated `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)`. The proxy begins a transaction and binds a connection to the thread.

**Step 2.** The method marks EMI-001 as PROCESSED and saves it, so the change is pending in the transaction but not yet committed.

**Step 3.** The payment gateway throws a checked `PaymentGatewayException`. Because `rollbackFor = Exception.class` is set, the proxy treats this checked exception as a rollback trigger rather than committing.

**Step 4.** The proxy rolls back the transaction. The PROCESSED mark on EMI-001 is undone, so the data is not corrupted — the EMI is NOT falsely recorded as paid.

**Step 5.** For the process-all path, the loop calls the extracted `EmiProcessorService` bean through its injected reference, so each call goes through the proxy and runs in a real transaction, avoiding the self-invocation trap entirely.

```
INFO  [exec-1] FixedEmiService - EMI-001 marked PROCESSED (pending in TX)
SEVERE[exec-1] FixedEmiService - PaymentGatewayException (checked) → rollbackFor triggers ROLLBACK
INFO  [exec-1] FixedEmiService - EMI-001 restored to PENDING (no corruption)
INFO  [exec-2] EmiProcessorService - process-all via separate bean → real TX per EMI
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are four cases where Transactional silently fails to rollback. First, checked exceptions: only RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback by default. A checked exception like IOException causes the proxy to COMMIT, potentially corrupting data. Fix with rollbackFor equals Exception.class. Second, self-invocation: calling a Transactional method from within the same class via this.method() bypasses the proxy because the call goes directly to the real object. Fix by extracting the method to a separate Service bean. Third, private methods: CGLIB creates a subclass proxy and cannot override private methods, so the annotation is silently ignored. Fix by making the method public. Fourth, swallowed exceptions: catching an exception without re-throwing makes the proxy think the method succeeded, so it commits. Fix by re-throwing or calling setRollbackOnly on the current transaction status.

In my EMI payment service, I demonstrated all four pitfalls with their fixes. The checked exception pitfall is the most dangerous because data corruption happens silently — the EMI is marked as processed but the payment actually failed. Adding rollbackFor equals Exception.class is a standard practice on every Transactional annotation in our codebase. The self-invocation pitfall is the most common — developers expect the annotation to work on any call, not realizing that the proxy only intercepts calls from outside the class.

---

### 8.4 (Q12 of 29)

keyPoints: Checked exception: does NOT rollback by default — must add rollbackFor
Self-invocation: this.method() bypasses proxy — no TX behavior
Private method: proxy cannot intercept — annotation ignored
Caught exception: if you catch and swallow, Spring sees no exception
